html:
A chain of walls, forts and watchtowers along the northern edge of China, built over two thousand years to hold back the peoples of the steppe. It is not one wall but many, raised and abandoned by different dynasties along different lines.

The first walls went up in the 7th century BCE, when the states of the Zhou world fenced off their borders against each other and against the north. After Qin unified China in 221 BCE, the First Emperor, Qin Shi Huang, had the northern walls joined into one frontier. The Han pushed the line far west into the Gansu corridor to guard the routes later called the Silk Road against the Xiongnu.

Most of what visitors see today is Ming work. After the Mongols were driven out in 1368, and especially after Mongol raids in the 16th century, the Ming rebuilt long stretches in brick and stone, with towers for smoke and fire signals.

The wall did more than defend:

  • It controlled who came and went, and taxed goods moving along the trade routes.
  • Its garrisons and roads made it a corridor for troops and supplies.
  • It marked, roughly, where farmland gave way to grassland.

It did not always work. The Mongols broke through in the 13th century, and in 1644 a Ming general opened the pass at Shanhaiguan to the Manchus, who founded the Qing.
sum: A chain of walls, forts and watchtowers along the northern edge of China, built over two thousand years to hold back the peoples of the steppe. It is not one wall but many, raised and abandoned by different dynasties along different lines.
